content:
Public talk about Muslims and the West runs on guesses. Some writers say Muslims are about to overwhelm Europe. Others say Islam is fading. Pew Research Center published a count in June 2025 that covers 2010 to 2020, and it gives the arguments something to stand on.

These seven figures come straight from that report and its companion on the wider religious landscape. Each one has a limit, and I mark the limits as I go.

Pew counts 2.0 billion Muslims in 2020, a rise of 21% in ten years. The rest of the world grew by about 10% over the same period.[1] Muslims now make up 25.6% of humanity, up from about 23.8% in 2010, and the increase of 347 million is larger than the increase of all other religious groups put together.[2]

Pew calls Muslims the fastest-growing religious group of the decade. A count of that size has margins of error, and Pew draws it from census and survey data that differ in quality from country to country.

Pew attributes the increase mainly to natural increase, because Muslims have a young age structure and higher fertility than most groups.[2] Switching religion has a small effect on the totals. Muslims are one of the few groups in which more people join than leave, but the numbers who switch in either direction are low.[2]

The report therefore gives no support to the claim that Muslim growth comes from mass conversion, and none to the claim that Muslims are leaving in large numbers.

Asia and the Pacific hold 59% of the world's Muslims. The Middle East and North Africa hold about one in five.[1] A third of all Muslims live in Indonesia, Pakistan or India, and Indonesia alone has about 240 million, roughly 12% of the total.[1]

Western debates often use "Muslim" and "Arab" as if they were the same word. The numbers show a religion whose centre of population sits in South and Southeast Asia.

India has 213 million Muslims, which is 15% of its population.[1] The ten countries with the most Muslims together hold 1.3 billion people, or 65% of the world total, and nine of the ten are Muslim-majority states.[1]

India is the exception on that list. One of the largest Muslim communities on earth lives as a minority under a non-Muslim majority.

Sub-Saharan Africa has 369 million Muslims, up 34% since 2010. They are 33% of the region's population and hold 18% of the world's Muslims, two points more than in 2010.[1]

Pew also records cases where the Muslim share fell. In Tanzania, Muslim women averaged 4.6 children against 5.5 for all women, and the Muslim share fell by 6 points.[1] Higher fertility is therefore not a rule for every Muslim population.

Muslims make up 6% of Europe's population, up 0.7 points from 2010.[1] North America has 5.9 million Muslims, which is a rise of 52% and the fastest growth of any region, from a small base.[1]

In Sweden the Muslim share rose by 4 points, in Austria by 3 and in Germany by 1. Pew links the modest increases in those three countries partly to Syrian refugees.[1] Pew adds that Muslim fertility in several European countries is higher than average.

Christians fell below half of the population in the United Kingdom (49%) and France (46%) during the decade, and the Netherlands now has a religiously unaffiliated majority (54%).[2] In the United States the Christian share dropped from 78.3% to 64.0%, while the unaffiliated share rose from 16.5% to 29.7%.[2]

A Muslim share of 6% in Europe sits against a falling Christian share and a growing unaffiliated one. The largest shift in Western religion over the decade was the rise of the unaffiliated.

The bottom line

The 2020 count describes a religion of 2 billion people whose centre sits in Asia, whose growth comes mainly from births, and whose share in Europe is 6%. Projections for the West depend on assumptions about migration and fertility, so anyone who quotes a figure should say who counted it and for which year.

Notes

  1. Pew Research Center, "Muslim population change", in How the Global Religious Landscape Changed from 2010 to 2020 (9 June 2025), https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/06/09/muslim-population-change/. Pew draws on the UN World Population Prospects (2024 revision) and the UN 2022 migrant stock estimates.
  2. Pew Research Center, How the Global Religious Landscape Changed from 2010 to 2020 (9 June 2025), https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/06/09/how-the-global-religious-landscape-changed-from-2010-to-2020/.
